title: Sandals on the throne
hookLine: for fourteen years, the most powerful thing in Ayodhya is a pair of shoes
carry: the sacred feet: bowing sets the ego down
last: SATYA: RAMA KEEPS HIS FATHER'S WORD.

lines: THE SANDALS CARRIED ON HIS HEAD.
A CITY LIKE A MOONLESS NIGHT.
cards: Bharata carries the sandals home on his head. That's how Valmiki describes it: not in a box, not under his arm, but raised on his head, the way you'd carry something sacred.
The army and the mothers follow, back through the places on the road. Ayodhya, when they reach it, looks to him like a dark night without a moon. And Bharata doesn't go into the palace.

teach.b: He goes to Nandigrama, a village just outside the city, and sets the sandals on the throne. He holds the royal umbrella over them himself.

When business comes, a dispute, a gift, a decision, he lays it before the sandals first, then acts as their servant. He wears bark and matted hair, as Rama does in the forest, and sleeps on the ground.
Fourteen years of ruling a kingdom and refusing to be its king. Why sandals? In Hindu worship, the feet are where you meet the holy.
Devotees bow at the feet of a god's image.
Temples and homes honor padukas, the sandals of Rama or of a revered teacher.

And children touch their elders' feet to ask a blessing. The feet are the lowest part of a person, so bowing to them means setting your own ego down. A prince carrying shoes on his head is that teaching, acted out.
Meanwhile, Rama leaves Chitrakoot, now full of memories, and the sages warn that demons are troubling the hermitages.
The three stop at the hermitage of the sage Atri and his wife Anasuya, an elderly ascetic well-known for her austerity, who gives Sita a garland, ornaments and an ointment that will never fade.
That's where the Ayodhya Kanda ends: sandals on a throne, and three people walking deeper into the trees.

how: Nandigrama is still visited by pilgrims near Ayodhya, and in many temples and homes Rama's sandals are honored as a sign of his presence.

o: Rama's sandals, set on the throne while Bharata serves them
a gold crown Bharata places on Rama's head in exile
a palace seat left empty until Kaikeyi chooses a king

games.q: the sacred feet — tap the pairs.
p: asking a blessing, ego set down

s: Bharata rules from the palace in Ayodhya
he rules from Nandigrama, outside the city, in bark and matted hair.
Bharata lays business before the sandals first
he acts as their servant, not as king.
Rama stays on Chitrakoot for all fourteen years
he leaves, and the third book follows him deeper into the forest.

games.q: you're Bharata, a prince, holding Rama's sandals. how do you carry them home?
o: on your head, as something holy.
in a locked box on a chariot.
games.why: on his head. in Hindu worship the feet, and what they've touched, are honored, and bowing to them sets the ego down.

practice: If you pray, bow now, forehead toward the floor or hands folded, and ask a blessing from someone you honor, God, a teacher, an elder, living or gone.
If you don't pray, simply lower your head a little and picture someone whose example you'd carry, the way Bharata carried those sandals. Stay there, small and steady, for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: The sandals. At Nandigrama, Bharata sets Rama's padukas on the throne and rules as their servant for fourteen years.

orig.note: Sanskrit nandigrāma: the village where Bharata rules in Rama's name.

carryVoice: Your line: the sacred feet, bowing sets the ego down. Bharata carried shoes on his head and served them for fourteen years. Day five hundred forty-nine.
